Do Boundary Tokens Delay the Accuracy Cliff?

Large language models are strikingly good at short deterministic tasks and then fail almost completely once the input gets long enough — an accuracy cliff. This project tests one proposed fix: chopping the input into visual “cells” with a structural marker like |. Does it actually delay the cliff, and if so, why?

Qwen2.5-7B — complete, 9 experiments Qwen2.5-14B — running (scale check) Mistral-7B — running (architecture check)
01

The problem: a cliff, not a slope

Ask an LLM to do a simple, mechanical transformation — shift every letter forward in the alphabet, keep a running sum, add two numbers — and something odd happens as the input gets longer. Accuracy doesn’t degrade smoothly. It holds up fine, then collapses.

Base (no boundary markers) Cellular (periodic | markers)

This isn’t a made-up worry. A recent paper — “How Focused Are LLMs?” (Hou et al., arXiv:2511.00763) — measured this cliff precisely across several frontier models and found it follows a specific mathematical shape (more on that below). A second paper, “Keeping LLMs Focused,” proposed a fix: insert periodic structural boundary tokens into the input, and the cliff moves further out. This project is a from-scratch replication and stress-test of that second paper’s claim.

| | |
02

The idea being tested

Take a task like “shift every letter forward in the alphabet” on the string ABCDEFGH. The Base condition gives the model that string as-is. The Cellular condition inserts a marker every few characters: ABCD|EFGH. The model is told the marker carries no meaning and to copy it through unchanged — it’s pure visual/structural scaffolding, not a hint about the answer.

The question: does chopping a long sequence into short visual chunks help the model’s attention stay organized, the way page breaks or paragraph indents help a human reader track a long document?

03

The theory behind the numbers

Every accuracy number in this project gets fit to a specific curve borrowed from statistical physics — a spin-glass model, the same mathematics used to describe disordered magnetic materials, repurposed here to describe how errors compound token-by-token.

The core equation

SAR(N) = exp(−β0 · N · αN−1)

SAR is the chance the model gets a whole sequence of length N completely right — the strict, all-or-nothing pass/fail metric. TAR is its softer cousin: per-character accuracy.

β0
Intrinsic error rate — roughly, how often the model slips on a single token in isolation.
α
Error-accumulation factor. α = 1 means errors don’t compound — ordinary exponential decay. α > 1 means each error makes the next one more likely, which is what actually produces a cliff instead of a slope.
N*
The cliff location — the sequence length where accuracy has effectively collapsed. Computed from β0 and α.

The whole project’s central question, restated in this language: does inserting boundary markers lower α? If it does, that’s a real, mechanistic reason the cliff moves out — not just an accuracy bump at one particular length.

04

The experiments

Nine angles of attack on the same question, run on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (with 14B-scale and a different model family, Mistral-7B, checked in parallel).

Strong
Cyclic shift
The home task: shift every letter forward in a fixed alphabet. Purely position-local — each output only depends on its matching input character, no cross-position dependency at all.
Mixed
Running sum mod M
Track a running cumulative sum through the sequence. Genuine global state, unlike cyclic shift — tests whether the effect survives when the task actually needs memory.
Negative
Integer addition
Add two multi-digit numbers, carries and all. The paper's own suite includes this; needs real digit-stream parsing and carry propagation.
Mixed
Addition, reversed digit order
Same task, digits written least-significant-first — testing whether boundaries hurt because they cut against carry-propagation direction.
Strong
Boundary ablation
Does the marker character matter? Does regular spacing matter, or just having some boundaries? Does density matter more than raw count? Three sub-questions, one grid.
Pending
Model scale: 7B vs 14B
Same Qwen family, bigger model. Does the boundary effect hold, strengthen, or vanish as parameter count grows?
Pending
Model family: Qwen vs Mistral
A same-size (~7B) model from a different architecture family — tests whether the attention-sink mechanism is Qwen-specific or general.
Strong
Prompt-wording robustness
Three differently-worded instruction templates for the same task, to rule out the effect being an artifact of one specific phrasing.
Strong
Error-containment & significance
Does the model recover faster right after crossing a boundary? And are the accuracy differences actually statistically significant, not just a positive-looking slope?

06

What we actually know so far

Weighing all nine experiments together, honestly — including the ones that didn’t work.

Solid

✓

Cyclic-shift is the strongest result

α drops 10–24% depending on alphabet size (bigger for 4/8-letter alphabets than 2-letter). The densest boundary spacing essentially eliminates the cliff for the 2-letter case (α ≈ 1.00). Backed by a real error-recovery signal (+5.7pp right after crossing a boundary), 31/54 statistically significant conditions, and it holds across three different phrasings of the instructions.

✓

Boundary density and regularity both matter, not just presence

With 20 trials and a proper paired significance test: random placement of the same number of boundaries is significantly worse than evenly-spaced placement (p<0.005 at every length ≥16). A fixed count of boundaries (density falling as the sequence grows) starts competitive at short lengths but falls significantly behind constant-density spacing as length increases. Marker identity (| vs ; vs #) made no significant difference — consistent with a generic attention-sink mechanism rather than something specific to the pipe character.

Genuinely mixed or negative — and informative because of it

∼

Modsum: the effect doesn’t show up when the task needs real global state

A running sum has a genuine dependency the boundary markers can’t address (they’re cosmetic, not resets). Error-recovery is ~0, zero statistically significant whole-sequence results, and the physics-model fit has no valid comparison at all — the model never completed a boundary-condition sequence perfectly, at any length tested. This is a real scope condition, not a failed replication.

×

Addition: boundaries actively hurt, and it’s not fully understood why

With 20 trials, Cellular scores dramatically worse than Base at every tested length (e.g. 7% vs 89% at N=4). A hypothesis — that left-to-right boundaries sever the right-to-left carry-lookback the model needs — was tested by reversing digit order to match carry direction. Both Base and Cellular got worse in absolute terms (the model is generally worse at reversed-order arithmetic), and Cellular stayed behind Base at every length, so the hypothesis wasn’t cleanly confirmed. It also wasn’t cleanly refuted — the relative gap narrowed. Inconclusive, flagged as needing real follow-up rather than a headline claim either way.

Open

?

Does this hold at 14B parameters, and on a different model family?

Both runs are in progress. This is the single most important open question — everything above was measured on one 7B model. If the effect replicates on Qwen2.5-14B and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, the cyclic-shift result graduates from “true of one model” to genuine evidence of a general mechanism.
